title: Commodities
text: Commodities are physical things, such as oil, metals and crops, but most of their price discovery happens in futures. Behind every contract sits a warehouse, a pipeline or a ship.

title: The profile
text: Here is the profile. What trades: energy, metals and farm products, mostly as futures and options. Who trades: producers and consumers who hedge, merchants, funds and electronic market makers. Where: on exchanges such as CME Group's NYMEX and COMEX, ICE, the London Metal Exchange and the Chinese exchanges, plus physical deals over the counter. Market data is each exchange's feed, plus official daily settlement prices. Front months trade electronically and fast, while later months are thinner. Futures clear centrally, and at expiry many of them deliver the physical good. FIA counted about 3.8 billion energy contracts, 3.8 billion in metals and 2.9 billion in agriculture traded in 2025.

title: Delivery and the curve
text: The distinctive feature is delivery, and with it the forward curve. Each delivery month has its own price, and the gaps between months reflect the cost of storing and financing the good. When later months trade higher, the curve is in contango. When nearby months trade higher, because the good is scarce now, it is in backwardation. NYMEX light sweet crude, for example, is 1,000 barrels, delivered at Cushing, Oklahoma.

title: April 20, 2020
text: Delivery can bite. On April 20, 2020, the day before the May WTI contract expired, it settled at minus 37.63 dollars a barrel, falling from 17.73. CFTC staff listed concerns about crude storage among the factors. At a negative price, a seller pays the buyer to take the contract. On one contract of 1,000 barrels, that is 37,630 dollars to hand it over.

title: When rules change
text: Rules can bite too. In March 2022, as nickel prices surged, the London Metal Exchange suspended nickel and cancelled every trade done on or after midnight UK time on March 8. For an algorithm, fills can be undone after the fact. The lab can rehearse this. Its simulated exchange has a break-at option that breaks the latest trade and publishes an ITCH broken trade message with the match number.

title: Traps
text: Some traps. Contract units range from barrels to bushels to tonnes, so check every multiplier. Do not hold a deliverable contract into delivery unless you can take the goods. Some contracts have daily price limits that can stop trading. And physical events, such as weather, pipelines and sanctions, move prices in jumps.

title: Takeaway
text: Commodities are futures with a warehouse behind them. Know the delivery terms, read the curve, and plan for the day the rules change.
